props.title: Woyzeck
props.initialSlug: Soldier's descent into madness and murder

sections.content: Werner Herzog's Woyzeck represents one of the most haunting adaptations of Georg Büchner's unfinished play, anchored by Klaus Kinski's raw, unhinged performance as the tormented soldier Franz Woyzeck. Shot in just 18 days immediately after Nosferatu the Vampyre (1979), Herzog channels the stark madness of German Expressionism while crafting an intimate portrait of psychological deterioration. The film's cold, desaturated palette and oppressive architecture mirror Woyzeck's mental prison, while Herzog's trademark long takes force us to witness his descent without escape.

sections.content: The film sits within Herzog's broader exploration of obsession and madness, particularly through his volatile collaboration with Klaus Kinski. Their five-film partnership, including Aguirre, the Wrath of God (1972) and Fitzcarraldo (1982), consistently pushed both director and actor to psychological extremes. In Woyzeck, Kinski channels a quieter but no less intense mania, his bulging eyes and twitching movements suggesting a man crushed by military discipline and social hierarchies.

Herzog's adaptation draws clear lines to other European art films examining institutional power and mental breakdown, from The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari (1920) to One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest (1975). The director's documentary-like attention to Woyzeck's degradation through medical experiments and military drills creates an atmosphere of clinical cruelty that influenced later films like Full Metal Jacket (1987) and The Piano Teacher (2001). sections.content: Herzog's stark visual approach in Woyzeck marked a significant departure from the sweeping landscapes of his earlier works. The cramped streets and claustrophobic interiors of the Czech filming locations create a suffocating atmosphere that would influence later psychological thrillers like Repulsion (1965) and The Tenant (1976). The film's use of handheld cameras during Woyzeck's episodes of paranoia established techniques that would become standard in depicting mental instability on screen.
